newsitem.title: USA: Long-sought 1960s radical nabbed in France.
newsitem.headline: Long-sought 1960s radical nabbed in France.

text.p: A 16-year international manhunt for a 1960s-era counterculture leader convicted of murdering his girlfriend has ended with his arrest in France, the FBI said on Monday.

Ira Einhorn, who fashioned a role for himself as a link between hippies and the establishment, was arrested on Friday at the converted windmill in southern France where he was living under an assumed name.
"He's now in custody in Bordeaux, France," Bob Reutter, FBI special agent in charge of the Philadelphia office, told a news conference.

Einhorn, now 57, jumped bail and fled Philadelphia in 1981, shortly before he was to go to trial for the 1977 murder of his girlfriend, Helen Maddux. Her mummified body had been found in 1979 in a steamer trunk at Einhorn's home. He had pleaded innocent to the killing, saying he had been framed.

Tried in abstentia in 1993, Einhorn was convicted, and sentenced to a term of life in prison without parole. An appeal by his attorney was denied on the grounds Einhorn had forfeited any rights to appeal by his absence.
The authorities said Einhorn could be returned within 40 days under terms of a U.S.-French extradition treaty, but legal battles could drag out the process.

Einhorn's attorneys said Monday they would ask France and, if necessary, the European Court of Human Rights to deny extradition on the grounds that it was unfair to try him without his presence and subsequently deny an appeal.
Einhorn was a leading figure on the Philadelphia counter-counterculture scene in the late 1960s and 1970s.
A friend of radicals Abbie Hoffman and Jerry Rubin, Einhorn portrayed himself as a peaceful promoter of social change. He was distinguished by a burly build, long hair, and a disdain for bathing.
Einhorn organised events such as Be-Ins and Love-Ins and helped found the University of Pennsylvania's Free University, and advised corporate leaders on intellectual trends.
In 1988, a book entitled "The Unicorn's Secret" was published about his life and flight, and contended that Einhorn's New Age aura was tarnished by a long history of violence toward women.
